topic: Mastering Wordle: Information Theory and Optimal Guessing Strategies
target_audience: University students with an interest in computer science and data analytics

outline.topic: Mastering Wordle: Information Theory and Optimal Guessing Strategies
outline.target_audience: University students with an interest in computer science and data analytics

sections.title: Introduction: The Goal and The Constraints
sections.content: Define Wordle as a hidden information game. Explain that in a 5-letter word game with 26 letters, the goal is to maximize information gain per turn to narrow down the search space.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Wordle-bot' (like a clever Fox) trying to guess a secret password. It has 2,315 possible solutions but 12,972 possible guesses.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Entropy and Information Gain
sections.content: Introduce Shannon Entropy as a measure of uncertainty. Explain that an optimal guess is one that splits the remaining possibility space into the most balanced groups.
sections.example: Visualizing a probability tree: A bad guess keeps 1,000 possibilities (high uncertainty); a 'high-entropy' guess splits the tree into many small, equal branches.

sections.title: Algorithm in Action: Frequency Analysis
sections.content: Demonstrate why 'CRANE' or 'SLATE' are statistically superior. Use a bar chart visualization showing letter frequency rankings in the English language (e.g., E, A, R, I, O are high frequency).
sections.example: A heatmap visual: The word 'CRANE' lights up the grid because it covers high-frequency consonants (R, N) and the most common vowels (A, E) simultaneously.

sections.title: Strategy Comparison: Hard Mode vs. Information Maximization
sections.content: Contrast 'Hard Mode' (must use clues found) vs. 'Information Mode' (guessing words to eliminate letters even if they aren't the answer). Show the trade-off between solving speed and accuracy.
sections.example: A robot character deciding between guessing 'ABBEY' (a potential win) vs 'TRACE' (an information-gathering sacrifice to eliminate 5 common letters).

sections.title: Conclusion: The Limit of Optimal Strategy
sections.content: Summarize the 'Minimax' algorithm approach—minimizing the maximum number of words remaining after a guess. Reiterate that the best strategy is the one that reduces the most 'branches' of the tree.
sections.example: A final visual of a narrowing funnel: Starting with 12,972 options, filtering through the 'Optimal Guess' filter, and funneling down to the singular correct answer.
